title: Climate action and 2023 tax levies approved
subtitle: Green development standards, University Avenue Gateway agreements, borrowing limits, neighbourhood levies and support for Bill 5 on harassment by local leaders.
overview: Council spent much of the afternoon on climate and sustainability. It received the 2020 regional greenhouse gas inventory and a regional green development standards update, both for information. It also approved the first annual sustainability and climate change report, reaffirmed the 2019 climate emergency, and directed staff to report back annually on emissions targets {{vote:m8}}.

On finances, Council adopted the 2023 general tax levy based on a final municipal levy of $92,656,663 {{vote:m10}}. It also approved the Uptown Waterloo BIA levy of $709,879 {{vote:m11}}, temporary borrowing authority of up to $97,540,637 {{vote:m2}}, and special service levies for four neighbourhood homes associations. The Mayor declared a conflict on the Glasgow II levy and left the room for that vote.

Council authorized agreements with Wilfrid Laurier University and the Region for the University Avenue Gateway project {{vote:m13}}. It also endorsed provincial Bill 5, which would strengthen codes of conduct on harassment for local leaders {{vote:m15}}. For residents, these decisions set 2023 property tax levies and advance public space and climate work.

decisions.detail: Council adopted the 2023 General Levy By-law based on a final municipal levy of $92,656,663.
Council approved the first annual report, reaffirmed the 2019 climate emergency and asked staff to report annually on corporate and community greenhouse gas targets.

The Mayor and Clerk may sign a contribution agreement with Wilfrid Laurier University for its outdoor public space, and future streetscape agreements with the Region, subject to funding and solicitor approval.
Council endorsed Bill 5, Stopping Harassment and Abuse by Local Leaders Act, and asked the Province to approve it, with copies of the motion sent to provincial and municipal bodies.
Council approved temporary loans, if required, up to $97,540,637 for 2023 expenditures and asked staff to report back on any borrowing.
Council approved a 2023 special levy of $709,879 to fund the Uptown Waterloo Business Improvement Area.
Council approved a 2023 levy of $24,000 for the Glasgow II Homes Association recreation facility and programs.
Council received the report on the region-wide green development standards project, Phase 2, for information.

debate: On the greenhouse gas inventory, a delegate said transportation remains the largest and growing source of emissions, and that 2020 reductions were largely due to pandemic effects. The delegate said retrofits, active transportation and advocacy to senior governments are priorities.

Councillors asked how to cut reliance on natural gas. Delegates said that changes such as phasing out gas appliances need provincial or federal action, and that the electricity grid needs upgrades to support electrification.

One councillor raised public pushback on cycling infrastructure and school drop-off traffic as obstacles to emissions-reducing decisions. Another asked whether private or public bodies are better placed to take bold climate action. Staff said municipal action must also consider equity and the public interest.

On green development standards, a councillor worried the one-to-two-year timeline is too slow given the pace of building. Staff and a delegate said the standards can build on other municipalities' work, but developers need lead time. Staff also noted possible provincial building code changes.
On Bill 5, one councillor supported it but noted that serious misconduct also occurs at provincial and federal levels. The Mayor agreed and said municipalities can show leadership.
